questions.stem: Which statement best defines a pathogen?

options.text: Any microorganism living in or on a human body
options.why: Many microorganisms in and on the body are harmless or beneficial. Disease-causing ability is what makes an agent a pathogen.

options.text: A disease-causing organism or infectious agent
options.why: Pathogens cause infectious disease. In this topic, the term mainly covers viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists.

options.text: Any foreign molecule that stimulates antibody production
options.why: That describes an antigen. An antigen is a molecule, while a pathogen is the disease-causing agent.

options.text: A bacterium that has developed antibiotic resistance
options.why: A resistant bacterium may be pathogenic, but resistance isn't part of the definition. Many pathogens aren't bacteria.

questions.stem: How do mucous membranes in the respiratory tract provide a primary defense?

options.text: They secrete antibodies that kill every inhaled pathogen
options.why: Antibodies belong to the adaptive response and are antigen-specific. Mucous membranes mainly prevent entry by trapping material.

options.text: They release antibiotics that block bacterial cell-wall production
options.why: Antibiotics are treatments directed at bacterial processes. They aren't the main protective secretion of a mucous membrane.

options.text: They trap pathogens in mucus, which cilia move toward the throat
options.why: Sticky mucus traps incoming material, and ciliary movement carries it away from vulnerable lung tissue.

options.text: They expose pathogens to plasma cells circulating through the airway
options.why: Plasma cells secrete antibodies after adaptive activation. This option misses the barrier function of mucus and cilia.

questions.stem: Which event directly produces the fibers of a blood clot?

options.text: Platelets convert fibrin into soluble fibrinogen
options.why: The direction is backwards. Soluble fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin.

options.text: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin
options.why: Fibrin forms the mesh that stabilizes the plug and traps erythrocytes at the wound.

options.text: Phagocytes digest fibrinogen and release clotting factors
options.why: Phagocytes digest foreign material. Platelets and damaged tissue supply clotting factors in this sequence.

options.text: Antibodies bind erythrocytes into an insoluble network
options.why: Antibodies bind specific antigens in adaptive immunity. Fibrin, rather than antibody, forms the clotting network.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to adaptive immunity but not innate immunity?

options.text: Recognition of broad categories of foreign material
options.why: That describes innate immunity. Its response isn't tailored to one particular antigen.

options.text: Engulfment of pathogens by phagocytic leucocytes
options.why: Phagocytosis is an innate response. It doesn't create antigen-specific memory.

options.text: A response that remains unchanged throughout life
options.why: That is characteristic of innate immunity. Adaptive responses improve after exposure because memory cells remain.

options.text: Retention of antigen-specific memory cells after exposure
options.why: Memory cells allow a faster and larger response when the same antigen appears again.

questions.stem: What happens during phagocytosis of a bacterium?

options.text: A phagocyte surrounds it, encloses it in a vesicle and digests it using lysosomal enzymes
options.why: Engulfment occurs by endocytosis, after which lysosomes supply hydrolytic enzymes to the vesicle.

options.text: A plasma cell surrounds it, encloses it in a nucleus and digests it using antibodies
options.why: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and don't engulf bacteria. Antibodies bind antigens rather than digesting pathogens.

options.text: A platelet surrounds it, traps it in fibrinogen and digests it using thrombin
options.why: Platelets and thrombin belong to clotting. They seal wounds rather than carrying out phagocytosis.

options.text: A helper T-cell surrounds it, encloses it in mucus and digests it using cytokines
options.why: Helper T-cells signal other immune cells using cytokines. They don't engulf pathogens or produce mucus.

questions.stem: What must happen before a specific B-lymphocyte is fully activated?

options.text: It must engulf any pathogen and receive a signal from a platelet
options.why: Engulfing broad categories of pathogen describes phagocytes. Platelets provide clotting factors, not B-cell activation.

options.text: It must bind a specific antibody and receive thrombin from a helper T-cell
options.why: A B-cell recognizes antigen, not an antibody supplied for activation. Helper T-cells release cytokines, not thrombin.

options.text: It must encounter its specific antigen and receive signals from a matching activated helper T-cell
options.why: Specific antigen recognition and helper T-cell contact and cytokines together activate the B-cell.

options.text: It must divide into plasma cells before it encounters a specific antigen
options.why: The order is reversed. Antigen recognition and helper signals activate the B-cell before clonal expansion and differentiation.

questions.stem: Why does an activated B-lymphocyte undergo repeated mitosis?

options.text: To produce many cells with the same antigen specificity
options.why: Clonal expansion creates enough matching cells to form antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory cells.

options.text: To produce antibodies with many unrelated antigen specificities
options.why: One activated clone keeps the same specificity. Different B-cell types are needed for unrelated antigens.

options.text: To turn the pathogen into a harmless memory cell
options.why: Memory cells are host lymphocytes, not modified pathogens. They remain after the response.

options.text: To replace helper T-cells destroyed during every infection
options.why: B-cell cloning supplies B-cell descendants. It doesn't replace a different lymphocyte type.

questions.stem: Why is the secondary immune response usually faster than the primary response?

options.text: The innate immune system permanently changes after the first infection
options.why: The innate system doesn't develop antigen-specific memory. The difference comes from adaptive memory cells.

options.text: Antibiotics remain in the blood after the first infection
options.why: Immune memory doesn't depend on retained antibiotics. Antibiotics are external treatments for bacterial infections.

options.text: The pathogen loses all its antigens during the first infection
options.why: The later response still depends on recognition of the same antigen. Losing it would prevent that recognition.

options.text: Long-lived memory cells specific to the antigen are already present
options.why: These cells can expand rapidly and generate a larger antibody response after another exposure to the same antigen.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes HIV from AIDS?

options.text: HIV is a bacterium, while AIDS is the antibiotic used against it
options.why: HIV is a virus, and AIDS isn't a treatment. Antiviral medicines can suppress HIV.

options.text: HIV is a virus, while AIDS is the immune-deficiency syndrome it can cause
options.why: HIV destroys helper T-cells, and severe resulting loss of immune function is described as AIDS.

options.text: HIV is an antibody, while AIDS is the antigen to which it binds
options.why: Neither term names an antibody or antigen. One is a virus and the other is a syndrome.

options.text: HIV is an opportunistic infection, while AIDS is a helper T-cell
options.why: HIV causes the immune damage that permits opportunistic infections. AIDS isn't a type of cell.

questions.stem: Why can an antibiotic that blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis fail against a virus?

options.text: Viruses have cellulose cell walls that the antibiotic cannot enter
options.why: Viruses have no cell wall. Cellulose walls occur in plants, not viruses.

options.text: Viruses contain resistant plasma cells that remove the antibiotic
options.why: Plasma cells belong to the human immune system. They aren't components of viruses.

options.text: Viruses reproduce too quickly for any chemical treatment to work
options.why: Some antiviral medicines can suppress viral reproduction. Speed isn't why this antibiotic fails.

options.text: Viruses lack bacterial cell walls and use host cells to reproduce
options.why: The antibiotic's target is absent from a virus, so blocking bacterial wall synthesis can't stop viral replication.

questions.stem: A bacterial population contains a few resistant cells before antibiotic treatment. What will treatment most directly do?

options.text: Cause every bacterium to develop the same resistance mutation
options.why: Mutations aren't directed by need. Treatment selects among variants already present.

options.text: Kill more susceptible bacteria, increasing the resistant fraction
options.why: Differential survival leaves resistant bacteria to reproduce, so resistance becomes more common.

options.text: Make the patient’s cells resistant to later antibiotic doses
options.why: Resistance is a heritable bacterial characteristic. The patient's body isn't the evolving bacterial population.

options.text: Convert the antibiotic into a vaccine against the bacteria
options.why: Vaccines stimulate antigen-specific immune memory. An antibiotic acts directly on bacterial processes.

questions.stem: Which example is a zoonotic transmission route?

options.text: Rabies virus passing to a human through an infected dog’s bite
options.why: This is direct transfer of an infectious agent from another animal species to a human.

options.text: A resistance allele passing to daughter bacteria during binary fission
options.why: That is inheritance within a bacterial population. It isn't transfer of disease from an animal to a human.

options.text: HIV passing between humans through contaminated blood
options.why: This is human-to-human transmission. It doesn't describe the animal-to-human transfer required here.

options.text: An antibody passing from a plasma cell into blood plasma
options.why: That is antibody secretion inside one person. No infectious disease crosses between species.

questions.stem: How can a nucleic-acid vaccine lead to immune memory?

options.text: Its DNA or RNA codes for an antigen that stimulates an adaptive response
options.why: Host cells produce the antigen, allowing antigen-specific lymphocytes to respond and memory cells to form.

options.text: Its DNA permanently replaces the recipient’s genes for antibody production
options.why: Vaccination doesn't require permanent replacement of the recipient's genome. The nucleic acid supplies instructions for an antigen.

options.text: Its RNA acts as an antibiotic that destroys every bacterial pathogen
options.why: The vaccine stimulates adaptive immunity to a specific antigen. It isn't a broad antibacterial drug.

options.text: Its nucleic acid becomes a supply of ready-made memory cells
options.why: Memory cells are living lymphocytes produced by the immune response. Nucleic acid isn't converted into cells.

questions.stem: Cases in a city rise from 400 in week 1 to 500 in week 2. What is the percentage change?

options.text: 20% increase, calculated using 500 as the denominator
options.why: Percentage change uses the old value as the denominator. Dividing 100 by 500 gives the wrong reference.

options.text: 22.2% increase, calculated using the mean of both values
options.why: Using the mean calculates percentage difference. This question compares a new value with an old value over time.

options.text: 25% increase, calculated using 400 as the denominator
options.why: The increase is 100, and 100 divided by the original 400 is 0.25, or 25%.

options.text: 125% increase, calculated by dividing 500 by 400
options.why: That calculation shows the new value is 125% of the old value. The increase itself is 25%.
